episode_title: Buyback-and-Burn Explained: Why Most Burns Don't Shrink Supply
summary: Jules and Mira unpack why the industry's $19B in buyback-and-burn rarely reduces circulating supply, walking through BNB, MakerDAO, the emissions problem, the burned-minus-emitted test, and FLIP's buy-and-distribute model and June 2026 net-supply milestone.
hook: The crypto industry has burned over $19 billion worth of tokens, yet most 'deflationary' tokens still have more supply every year. Jules explains it with a bait shop owner named Dale, and Mira gives you the one subtraction that cuts through every burn announcement.
key_points: Why buyback-and-burn is popular, and why most tokens claiming deflation still saw supply grow year over year
How BNB's utility sinks and MakerDAO's burn-when-profitable, mint-when-not model complicate the burn story
The emissions problem: burning $10M a year while emitting $50M is 'inflationary with better marketing'
The simple test: tokens burned minus tokens emitted over a period
How buy-and-distribute works, and FLIP crossing burns-exceed-emissions on June 10, 2026

chapters.title: BNB and MakerDAO: big burns, mixed results
The emissions problem and the one calculation

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [grinning] Okay, the summer I worked at the bait shop, the owner, Dale, put a sign in the window. "We threw out a hundred dead minnows this week. Freshest tank in the county."

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: That's a choice of slogan.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: But that same week, the truck dropped off five hundred new minnows. The tank was more crowded than ever.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: [deadpan] So the tank grew by four hundred, and Dale advertised the hundred.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Dale was ahead of his time.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: [amused] Dale was running a token burn. Welcome to Cross-Chain Daily, I'm Mira, that's Jules, and today it's buyback-and-burn, and why so few tokens that burn actually end up with less supply.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Start me simple. What's a buyback-and-burn?

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: A protocol makes revenue, uses it to buy its own token off the market, and destroys those tokens. BNB, MKR, FTT before it collapsed, and dozens of others use some version of it.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: And the article says the whole industry has burned over nineteen billion dollars worth.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Over nineteen billion. And yet most tokens calling themselves deflationary saw circulating supply go up year over year.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Wait. Up?

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Up. That's the whole article in one word.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: So why does everybody love burns?

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Because they're visible. A burn is an on-chain event you can screenshot, so every one becomes a marketing moment. Nobody asks the boring follow-up: is circulating supply actually going down?

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Okay, so, um, give me the big one. BNB.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Largest burn program by dollar value. Quarterly burns, calculated from trading volume and other factors. Big numbers.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: But.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: But BNB is also gas on BNB Chain, it's used for Launchpad allocations, it has all these utility sinks. So what's really circulating depends on way more than burn math. Big burns don't automatically mean the supply drop retail pictures.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Then Maker. That one confused me.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: MKR runs a surplus buffer. Protocol's profitable, extra DAI buys and burns MKR. Protocol hits bad debt, new MKR gets minted and sold to cover it.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [half-laughing] So it's a burn with a refund policy.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Pretty much. Big burns in the profitable stretch of twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-three, but earlier liquidation events had already diluted supply. Over multiple years, the net is less dramatic than the announcements.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: And the article says that's a pattern.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Burn in good times, dilute in bad times. The burns get announced. The dilution happens quietly.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: I mean, that's Dale. That's exactly Dale.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: [dry] I'm starting to think Dale is the whole thesis.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: So where do the new minnows come from, in token land?

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Emissions. Validator rewards, liquidity incentives, team vesting, ecosystem grants. Those often outrun the burns by a lot. The article's example: burn ten million dollars a year while emitting fifty million in rewards.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: That's not deflation.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: In the article's words, it's inflationary with better marketing.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [grinning] That's going on a t-shirt. Right next to Dale's sign.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Burns get the headlines, emission schedules get buried in the docs. So "deflationary" has basically stopped meaning anything.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: So how does a normal person check? Someone with, honestly, a pretty rough trade history?

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: One calculation. Tokens burned minus tokens emitted over a period. Positive means real deflation. Negative means the burns are theater.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Burned minus emitted. That's it?

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: That's it. And for most tokens it's disappointing. Staking rewards alone often beat the yearly burn. Add incentives, team unlocks and grants, and the gap widens.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: So who actually passes?

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Tokens whose burns are funded by real protocol revenue that's bigger than what they need to emit.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Which gets us to the alternative. Buy-and-distribute?

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Instead of destroying tokens and hoping the price notices, you buy tokens and hand them straight to stakers. The article's example is Chainflip's FLIP, which moved from a pure burn to buy-and-distribute. Protocol revenue buys FLIP on the market and sends it to stakers as yield.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: So instead of tossing minnows, Dale hands them to his regulars.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Hmm. Okay, that one works. Stakers can measure exactly what they got. No hoping the market turns a burn into a price move.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [quick, cutting in] Write it down. Date it.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Noted. And there's a milestone. On June tenth, twenty twenty-six, FLIP's total tokens burned since launch passed total tokens emitted.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: So it actually shrank.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Net supply reduction. The point isn't that FLIP is uniquely virtuous, it's what happens when burns are sized right against emissions. The article cites over nine point five billion dollars in all-time swap volume generating steady fees, at the time of writing.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Okay. Checklist, so I stop getting Dale'd.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Four questions. Net supply: do burns beat emissions each year? Revenue source: real revenue or treasury spending? Emission schedule: what's the full picture entering circulation? Transparency: do they publish both burns and emissions clearly?

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: And most tokens...

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Fail more than one. The article says that nineteen billion includes billions in marketing spend dressed up as value accrual.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Ouch.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Good news is the market's growing up. People used to take burn announcements at face value. Now they want the math, and the data's free. On-chain data doesn't lie, even when marketing departments do.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: So the takeaway: don't count the minnows thrown out. Count the tank.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Burned minus emitted. The full article is linked in the show notes, and none of this is financial advice.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [grinning] Dale, if you're listening, no hard feelings. Stay native.

lore.note: Spent a summer at a bait shop run by Dale, who posted a sign bragging about throwing out a hundred dead minnows the same week five hundred new ones arrived. 'Getting Dale'd' is now Jules's phrase for falling for burn-style marketing.

Her one-number rule for any deflation claim: 'burned minus emitted.' She also admitted a second Jules analogy works (Dale handing minnows to his regulars as buy-and-distribute), and Jules again made her 'date it.'
